podcast.title: Founder of Creation Records
podcast.body: Alan McGee, a Scotsman, founded Creation Records in 1983, which carved out an important niche in the early 1980s indie movement. "It was founded by a Scotsman named Alan McGee in 1983."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Key Discoveries and Financial Outcome
podcast.body: McGee's significant early contribution was signing The Jesus and Mary Chain. He later discovered and signed Oasis, another band with "brawling, hard to deal with brothers." Despite Creation Records facing money issues, including a near-bankruptcy due to a costly My Bloody Valentine record, McGee eventually sold the label to Sony. "McGee's best early contribution was signing the Jesus and Mary Chain."

xref.title: Discovery at King Tut's Wah Wah Hut (1993)
xref.body: Oasis was allegedly discovered by Alan McGee of Creation Records at King Tuts Wah Wah Hut on St. Vincent Street in Glasgow, Scotland, on May 31, 1993. This event purportedly occurred after the band threatened the owner with arson if they were not allowed to perform that night. "Oasis was discovered by Alan McGee of creation records after they allegedly threatened the owner with arson if he didn't let them play that night."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Forced Performance and Record Deal at King Tuts Wawa Hut (May 31, 1993)
xref.body: On Sunday, May 31, 1993, Oasis, who were not scheduled to play, physically "bullied their way on stage" for a set at King Tuts Wawa Hut in Glasgow, Scotland. Having hitched a ride with another Manchester group, 18 Wheeler, they threatened the venue's owner and bouncers with burning down the club if they weren't allowed to perform. Coincidentally, Alan McGee of Creation Records was present, initially to see other bands on the bill, but was so impressed by Oasis that he signed them "more or less on the spot," later lending them £1,000 for equipment. "Oasis literally bullied their way on stage for a set at King Tuts Wawa Hut in Glasgow, Scotland."

xref.title: Connection to Creation Records
xref.body: A demo tape from the band fortuitously reached Alan McGee, the head of Creation Records, leading to the label releasing their single "Upside Down" and later their debut album. This connection was pivotal in their early career. "Through some happenstance, their demo tape came to the attention of Alan McGee and an indelabel called Creation Records."

xref.title: Expensive Record and Label Bankruptcy Threat
xref.body: My Bloody Valentine, one of Alan McGee's "proudest signings" to Creation Records, turned in a record that was "so expensive to make that it nearly bankrupted the label," highlighting the financial vulnerabilities of independent labels. "one of McGee's proudest signings, my bloody Valentine, turned in a record that was so expensive to make that it nearly bankrupted the label."

xref.title: Major Label Deal with Alan McGee
xref.body: In 2000, following their second album, "Vini Vidi Vicious," The Hives were signed by Alan McGee, the founder of Creation Records (who discovered Oasis), to his new label, Pop Tones. This deal led to a major label contract that some speculated was worth $50 million. "By 2000, Alan McGee had a new label called Pop Tones and he wanted The Hives. So he signed them. One thing led to another and suddenly, the Hives had a major label deal that some said was worth $50 million."
